statement: In the one study read here that measured it, at one US autopsy centre, full autopsy with drug testing changed which deaths were put down to drugs in both directions: the autopsy found another cause in some deaths suspected to be drug deaths, and testing found drug deaths among deaths nobody suspected. Access to testing differs widely between US offices, and no study read here measured the effect on official counts. At a regional autopsy centre serving 33 counties of western North Carolina (population 2,354,038), which kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug deaths in 2016–2021 when other offices had moved to an external examination with toxicology, investigators suspected before autopsy that 2,719 of 2,956 adult deaths were drug-related, from drug equipment at the scene, a history of substance use disorder or earlier overdoses. After full autopsy and comprehensive toxicology, the assigned pathologist gave a cause unrelated to drugs in 265 of them (9.75%), for example a blood clot in the lungs, a burst stomach ulcer, a burst brain aneurysm with no stimulants in the body, or a bleed pressing on the brain in a homicide. Because the 265 include deaths whose toxicology found no drug, which an external examination with toxicology would presumably not have put down to drugs, 9.75% is an upper limit (editors' reading) for what such an examination would have put down to drugs wrongly, among the suspected deaths only; the paper does not give the split. In the other direction, toxicology showed a drug cause, with no significant findings at autopsy, in 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation). The assigned pathologist's conclusion was the yardstick, illicit drugs found were counted as at least contributing unless a catastrophic natural or traumatic cause was found, and intentional (suicidal) drug overdoses, deaths with obvious fatal injuries and people under 18 were left out. The authors also say that scene investigation, external examination and comprehensive toxicology gave a correct determination in a majority of cases, and they summarize two other US studies, not read here: in one, toxicology found no drug and another cause was concluded in 11% to 13% of suspected drug deaths; in the other, three pathologists without internal examination findings got cause and manner right in 75% to 80% of 60 selected cases (Hancock et al., 2024). The National Association of Medical Examiners recommends an autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected (except delayed deaths after an overdose, when the hospital record is reviewed instead) and comprehensive toxicology for eight kinds of death; it states that history, investigation and autopsy together are an insensitive guide to intoxication and that no peer-reviewed study has shown an external examination to be as accurate as an autopsy, and it cites one study of drug deaths, without a figure, for external examination being less accurate even when the scene strongly suggests an overdose; its figure of 20% to 30% wrong diagnoses without autopsy comes from general autopsy studies, some decades old, and a mortality data brief, not from studies of drug deaths (Davis et al., 2020, a position paper). Access to testing varies: in the 2018 census of US medical examiner and coroner offices, as the offices reported it, of 1,320 offices that answered, 82.6% had access to toxicology (5.9% in-house, 76.7% through outside laboratories), 11.2% said they had none and 6.2% that they did not need it (the authors note that some offices without access may have their deaths tested through an autopsy provider or a state office); 96.4% of offices serving 250,000 people or more had access, against 75.1% of those serving fewer than 25,000; a coroner or other non-physician was the role most often named as deciding which deaths were tested (by 64.7% of offices; more than one role could be named); and 53.9% of 1,326 offices used drug screening tests, 95.1% of 709 of these confirming them in a laboratory. These are shares of offices, not of deaths: the authors state that the number of suspected overdose deaths actually tested is not known (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine US states in 2019–2021, a full or partial autopsy was recorded for about 67%, an opioid test for 79% and an alcohol test for 76%, with 'no' and 'unknown' counted together for the two tests (Lundberg et al., 2026). What is tested changes what is found: as a review reports, after routine testing for gabapentin began in Kentucky in July 2014, its share among drug overdose deaths rose from 2.9% in 2013 to 17% in 2014 (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand), and a US consensus panel noted in 2013 that many immunoassays used for screening did not detect some opioids, such as oxycodone and hydromorphone, and that laboratories used no standard detection threshold (Goldberger et al., 2013). Of 48 of Kentucky's 120 elected coroners who answered a survey in 2016, after state laws of 2012 and 2015 required toxicology testing, 58% reported more toxicology testing requested and 35% reported more autopsies; these are the coroners' own reports, and no death records were examined (Quesinberry et al., 2019). In Norway in 2007–2009, deaths without an autopsy had higher odds of being counted by the cause-of-death register but not by the police register (adjusted odds ratio 2.66) (Amundsen, 2017), and in Stockholm a register built from forensic toxicology could not include deaths without a forensic examination, such as the 151 hospital deaths in a local reference inventory of drug deaths (Fugelstad et al., 2020). How often deaths certified without autopsy or testing are wrongly put down to drugs, or missed, has not been measured in official statistics. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths? At one autopsy centre in North Carolina (2016 to 2021), investigators suspected that 2,719 deaths were drug deaths. After a full autopsy and drug tests, about 1 in 10 of them had another cause, such as a blood clot or a burst blood vessel in the brain. This is an upper limit for the suspected deaths, because it includes deaths where tests found no drug at all. Of 237 deaths nobody suspected, drug tests showed that about half were drug deaths. The authors say that most deaths would have been put down correctly from the scene, an outside examination of the body and full drug tests, without an autopsy. Testing differs a lot: in 2018, about 1 in 9 US death investigation offices said they had no access to drug testing (some may send deaths elsewhere for testing), and small offices had it less often than big ones. Medical examiners' guidance says to do an autopsy whenever a drug death is suspected, but the error figure it gives comes mostly from autopsy studies of all kinds of deaths. This rests mainly on one centre in one US state.
magnitude: North Carolina centre 2016–2021 (Hancock et al., 2024): suspected before autopsy 2,719 of 2,956; non-drug final cause in 265 (9.75%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 8.7% to 10.9%), an upper limit for external examination with toxicology among the suspected deaths only; not suspected 237, drug-related final cause shown by toxicology in 115 (48.5%, 42.2% to 54.9%, editors' calculation); printed sensitivity 95.52%, specificity 31.52%. Second-hand in the same paper (not read): 11% to 13% of suspected drug deaths with no drug found and another cause; 75% to 80% correct on cause and manner without internal examination in 60 selected cases. US 2018 census (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025), 1,320 offices: toxicology access 82.6% (in-house 5.9%, outside 76.7%), none 11.2%, not needed 6.2%; large offices 96.4%, small 75.1%; coroner or non-physician named among those deciding testing by 64.7% of offices; screening 53.9% of 1,326, laboratory confirmation 95.1% of 709; shares of offices, self-reported. Nine US states 2019–2021 (Lundberg et al., 2026): full or partial autopsy recorded about 67%, opioid test 79%, alcohol test 76% of 55,430. Second-hand: Kentucky gabapentin 2.9% (2013) to 17% (2014), routine testing from July 2014 (Slavova et al., 2019). Kentucky coroners 2016, 48 of 120: more toxicology 58.3%, more autopsies 35.4%, self-reported (Quesinberry et al., 2019). Norway 2007–2009: no autopsy, adjusted odds ratio 2.66 (1.42–4.98) for being counted only by the cause-of-death register (Amundsen, 2017). NAME's 20% to 30% error figure is from general autopsy studies and a mortality data brief (Davis et al., 2020).

risk_of_bias.note: The one direct comparison (card sc_hancock_2024: JBI moderate) uses the assigned pathologist's conclusion as the yardstick, which partly includes the investigation behind the suspicion and counts illicit drugs present as contributing, does not report how suspicion was classified or whether blind to the final cause, and mixes toxicology-negative deaths into its 265; the census describes what offices reported, with misclassification the authors document (card sc_smiley_mcdonald_2025: moderate).

inconsistency.note: Not rated: one direct comparison; the other sources describe testing practice and point the same way.

indirectness.note: One US regional centre that kept full autopsies, adults only, with suicides and obvious injuries left out; testing access and practice from the US in 2018 and nine states in 2019–2021. Nothing measures the effect of autopsy or testing on national counts, or practice outside the US apart from two Nordic register notes.

imprecision.note: 2,956 deaths; the 9.75% has an editors' interval of 8.7% to 10.9%.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: very low. The North Carolina series compares the same deaths before and after full autopsy and toxicology, the kind of comparison this question needs, and finds changes in both directions (another cause found at autopsy in suspected deaths; drug deaths found by testing among deaths not suspected); it is a single centre, its 9.75% is an upper limit, among suspected deaths only, for what external examination with toxicology would misattribute, and the two other US studies it summarizes are second-hand and not counted. The position paper (Davis et al., 2020) is cited for its recommendations and the origin of its error figure, not as evidence of an error rate; the Kentucky survey records coroners' own reports; the gabapentin figure is second-hand from a review. Status single study for the direct comparison. Whether the type of official who investigates matters is a separate, contested answer.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the kind of official who investigates a death changes how drug deaths are counted. In the US, deaths in counties served by coroners were more often recorded as of undetermined intent than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same states, and studies summarized second-hand found that certificates named no drug more often where coroners certify; but the one study of states that switched to medical examiner systems found no detectable improvement in how specifically poisoning deaths were coded, and across nine states taken together, without allowing for the state, the association with undetermined intent ran the other way; no study checked which records were right. A US consensus panel defines medical examiners as appointed, professionally trained forensic pathologists and coroners as elected or appointed officials whose qualifications vary widely (Goldberger et al., 2013); a later study describes medical examiners as typically appointed physicians and coroners as elected laypeople, with requirements varying by state, some states requiring coroners to be physicians (Lundberg et al., 2026). In Kentucky, for example, a coroner must be at least 24 years old and meet residence rules, no training in medicine or forensic pathology is required, and new coroners must complete 40 hours of basic training; of 48 coroners who answered a 2016 survey, 47 held another job, 28 as funeral directors (Quesinberry et al., 2019). In the 2018 census of US offices, about 80% were in coroner systems (a figure the authors quote from the Bureau of Justice Statistics report), coroners or other non-physicians were the role most often named as deciding which deaths were tested (64.7% of offices), and offices serving fewer than 25,000 people less often reported access to toxicology (75.1%, against 96.4% of offices serving 250,000 or more), a comparison by population served, not by type of office (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine states in 2019–2021, deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as of undetermined intent, rather than as an accident or a suicide, than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same state and year (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.27; 1.52 to 1.61 after allowing for county characteristics, recorded investigation steps and the person's age, sex and race); without allowing for the state the odds were lower in coroner counties (0.32; 3.1% against 8.9% recorded as undetermined), which the authors attribute to Maryland, a state with a central medical examiner and many undetermined deaths, without showing a model that leaves Maryland out. The within-state comparison can draw only on states with both kinds of county, which excludes Indiana (coroners only) and North Carolina and Maryland (central medical examiners) (editors' inference from the authors' descriptions). An alcohol test was recorded for 58.6% of deaths in coroner counties against 84.5% in medical-examiner counties, while autopsies (about 68% and 67%) and opioid tests (about 80% and 79%) were recorded about equally often (editors' percentages), and whether a test was recorded was largely not associated with the classification, by the authors' account; the type of system was taken from a 2024 listing (Lundberg et al., 2026). A scoping review summarizes, second-hand, three studies that found more certificates naming no drug where coroners certify, one with odds ratios of 1.77 (2014) and 3.87 (2018) for an unclassified overdose death in coroner counties, and reports from another, a national analysis of 2008–2010, that the share of overdose deaths of undetermined manner varied by state but not by type of system (Gutkind et al., 2025); a commentary cites that analysis for the share of overdose certificates naming specific drugs, on average 92% in states with a central medical examiner, 73% in hybrid systems, 71% in local medical-examiner systems and 62% in coroner systems (Slavova et al., 2015, as cited); and a 2019 review reports that in 2016 the share of drug poisoning deaths recorded as of undetermined intent ranged from 1% in Connecticut and Massachusetts to 68% in Maryland, and suggests that office policies not aligned with professional recommendations may drive such differences (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited). Against this, seven states that switched to a medical examiner system in 1976–1996 (two of them from physician coroners or locally appointed physicians, two from justices of the peace), compared with seven states that did not, chosen for nearness and similar earlier trends, showed no detectable change in the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code (difference-in-differences −0.02 to −0.03, standard errors 0.04 to 0.06, so falls of 10 to 14 percentage points from a share near one half could not be ruled out, editors' calculation, with no stated allowance for repeated years of the same state), in data that ended in 1998 and included poisonings by substances other than drugs; the state pairs moved in different directions after the switch, which a pooled estimate can average out (Zaychik, 2024). See the contested question. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates? It is not clear. In the US, medical examiners are usually doctors appointed to the job; coroners are often elected, and in some states need no medical training. In nine US states (2019 to 2021), deaths in coroner areas were more often recorded without saying whether the death was an accident or a suicide than deaths in medical examiner areas of the same state. Other studies found that certificates named no drug more often where coroners work. But seven states that switched to medical examiners showed no clear change in how precisely poisoning deaths were recorded, although that study could not rule out a real improvement, and its data end in 1998. Nobody checked which records were right.
magnitude: Nine US states 2019–2021, undetermined intent in coroner against medical-examiner counties (Lundberg et al., 2026): within state and year, odds ratio 1.79 (1.43–2.27); adjusted 1.52 (1.20–1.95), 1.61 (1.26–2.06), 1.60 (1.25–2.05); pooled without state, 0.32 (0.29–0.35), 558 of 18,232 (3.1%) against 3,329 of 37,198 (8.9%); no within-state contrast in Indiana, North Carolina or Maryland (editors' inference). Alcohol test recorded 58.6% against 84.5% (editors' percentages). Second-hand: unclassified overdose deaths in coroner counties, odds ratios 1.77 (1.08–2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32–6.46) in 2018 (Gutkind et al., 2025); undetermined manner varied by state but not by system, 2008–2010 (Gutkind et al., 2025); certificates naming specific drugs 92% (central medical examiner), 73% (hybrid), 71% (local medical examiner), 62% (coroner) (Slavova et al., 2015); undetermined share of drug poisoning deaths in 2016, 1% to 68% (Slavova et al., 2019). Seven state switches 1976–1996 (Zaychik, 2024): difference-in-differences in the non-specific share −0.02 (SE 0.04), −0.03 (0.05), −0.02 (0.06); editors' 95% intervals −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07, −0.14 to 0.10, probably too narrow (no stated allowance for repeated state-years). US offices 2018: about 80% in coroner systems (as quoted from the Bureau of Justice Statistics); toxicology access 75.1% (small) against 96.4% (large) (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025).

risk_of_bias.note: The associations come from cross-sectional comparisons between counties or states that cannot separate the system from its resources and setting, with the system type taken from a later listing (card sc_lundberg_2026: ROBINS-E some concerns); the before-and-after study is at serious risk of bias from a pooled model, a coding revision inside most windows and an outcome that mixes non-drug poisonings (card sc_zaychik_2024: ROBINS-I serious); several figures are second-hand.

inconsistency.note: The within-state association and the second-hand associations on drugs named point one way; the pooled nine-state estimate, a second-hand national analysis of undetermined manner and the before-and-after study point the other way or show nothing detectable, and the explanations offered (Maryland's practice; different outcomes and eras) are not tested.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US data only, outcomes are how specifically deaths were recorded (undetermined intent, no drug named), not deaths missed, as the claim states.

imprecision.note: The within-state estimates have intervals above 1 (lowest limit 1.20); the before-and-after study's imprecision is stated in the claim and counted under inconsistency.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, which is below the floor: very low. Status contested: credible evidence points both ways, cross-sectional associations against the only before-and-after test and a reversed pooled estimate, so the six-part debate box applies. Counted once: the 92%, 73%, 71% and 62% figures appear in both reviews by the same first author (Slavova et al., 2015; 2019) and come from one earlier analysis (Warner et al., 2013, not read), which the scoping review (Gutkind et al., 2025) also summarizes; the scoping review is cited only for primary studies not read here, labelled second-hand. The Kentucky survey and the 2018 census describe who investigates and with what testing; they do not compare counts. Whether an autopsy or a drug test changes which deaths count as drug deaths is a separate answer.

statement: In one randomized online experiment with UK adults, details in a simulated news report of a drug death changed how much stigma readers said they felt towards the person who died, by small to moderate amounts, but hardly changed their stated support for harm-reduction policies. In June 2022, 1,248 adults on a UK online research panel (Prolific; mean age 45.7, 51.0% women) were each randomly assigned to read one of eight versions of a BBC-style news story about an inquest, adapted from a real BBC report of an ecstasy death in 2019; the versions differed in the person's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 and had used the drug 'once or twice', or 43 and had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin). Stigma towards the person, on a new nine-item measure of blame, anger, pity, responsibility, control and wish for distance (range 9 to 81), was higher when the person was a man (mean 45.6 against 43.4 for a woman), when the person was older with long use (46.7 against 42.3) and when the drug was heroin (46.9 against 42.1): about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations (editors' calculation), with the eight versions ranging from 38.6 (young woman, ecstasy) to 50.1 (older man, heroin). Support for six harm-reduction policies (such as drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone and opioid agonist treatment; range 6 to 30) was slightly higher after the older person's story (about 23.6 against 23.0, editors' calculation from the condition means, about 0.1 standard deviation; the paper prints the two means in reverse order), a difference seen in the ecstasy stories only (about 23.9 against 22.7, with none in the heroin stories, editors' calculation), and did not differ by drug or by gender. In exploratory, non-randomized analyses of 868 participants, stronger belief in a just world, less perspective-taking and more general stigma towards people with drug problems went with more stigma towards the person, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug death went with less (Sumnall et al., 2023). The study was not registered in advance, the stigma measure was new, the panel was matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented people with degrees and people who prefer left-wing parties, the outcomes were self-reports measured once straight after one written story, and 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'. How real news coverage affects behaviour, policy or the people affected was not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think? In one UK study, 1,248 adults online each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random. Readers judged the person more harshly when the person who died was a man, was 43 and had used the drug for years rather than 21 and had used it once or twice, and when the drug was heroin rather than ecstasy. These were small to moderate differences. Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed. Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; the study did not look at what they did later, and it could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using drugs for longer.
magnitude: Sumnall et al. (2023), 2 × 2 × 2 factorial, n = 1,248 (degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed). Stigma (9–81): man 45.6 (SD 12.1) against woman 43.4 (12.6), F(1,1230) = 11.1, p < .001; older with 15 years' use 46.7 (11.8) against younger, used once or twice, 42.3 (12.7), F = 40.5, p < .001; heroin 46.9 (11.5) against ecstasy 42.1 (12.8), F = 50.1, p < .001; editors' d about 0.18, 0.36 and 0.39; condition means 38.6 to 50.1. Harm-reduction support (6–30): age, F = 4.5, p = .035 (older about 23.6 against younger 23.0, editors' calculation; d about 0.12); in the ecstasy stories about 23.9 against 22.7 and in the heroin stories 23.3 against 23.3 (editors' calculation from Table 1); the F = 4.8, p = .029 printed with the ecstasy comparison recomputes as the age-by-drug interaction test (about 5.4), not the within-ecstasy difference (about 10) (editors' calculation); gender F = .0, p = .802; drug F = .0, p = .922. Exploratory regression (868 participants, editors' calculation from degrees of freedom): story factors R² = .068, final model R² = .569.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2, some concerns (card sc_sumnall_2023): not registered in advance, so the choice of total scores and analyses cannot be checked against a plan; a new stigma measure with only internal consistency reported; unreported exclusions implied by the degrees of freedom; and the age contrast also changed the use history, the brother's age and possibly the photographs.

indirectness.note: An online panel matched to the UK on sex, age and ethnicity only, one simulated written story read once, and self-reported attitudes measured straight away, rather than real news, other countries or what readers did later.

imprecision.note: 1,248 randomized; the main stigma differences are clear (F 11.1 to 50.1), and the harm-reduction differences are stated as very small.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one unregistered study.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb 'increases' rests on random assignment within the experiment and applies to stigma towards the depicted person; for support for harm-reduction policies the claim reports a very small difference by age with use history and no difference by drug or gender. The participant-trait associations come from non-randomized regressions on 868 participants and are reported as associations. Status single study; the authors report no earlier experiment on news depictions of drug deaths.

statement: In the UK mephedrone scare of 2009–2010, several deaths that online news linked to mephedrone were later reported not to have been caused by it, including the deaths most linked to it online; the evidence is one study of online news whose later toxicology is second-hand (as later reported, not taken from coroners' records), so its figures are illustrative. Searching Google News from 26 November 2009 to one year after the ban (enforced on 16 April 2010), the author found 18 named people whose deaths online news linked to mephedrone; suicides and violent or accidental deaths were left out, and their number is not given. Later reports said that mephedrone was not found in 4, including two young men in Scunthorpe, whose names were linked to mephedrone on about 9,060 and 8,730 web pages by June 2011 (more than any other case), who were reported a month after the ban not to have taken mephedrone, and whose inquest in 2011 found that they died from alcohol combined with methadone; that it was found but was not a factor in 4; and that it was a factor in 7, six of them with other drugs or illnesses also alleged. For 3 there was no later toxicology note, and the first death linked to mephedrone, of a 14-year-old girl in November 2009, was reported in local news within a month as due to natural causes (pneumonia after a streptococcal infection), yet went on being named as a mephedrone death in local, national and international news for months. The author reads the volume of news as showing that reports confirming that mephedrone was not responsible were far fewer than the earlier reports suggesting that it was. In screenshots of relative Google search indices without absolute numbers, searches for 'mephedrone' rose around the most-reported deaths and fell after the ban, and searches for 'mephedrone buy' rose far more after the Scunthorpe deaths than after the first death (no 'mephedrone buy' data are shown after 24 March 2010). The author reads this as suggesting a 'boomerang effect', news of drug deaths raising interest in the drug, including in buying it, while conceding that a search is not a purchase and that the data show neither how many people searched nor why; in the editors' reading, timing in screenshots cannot show that the news made people seek or use the drug (Forsyth, 2012). For comparison, the paper cites official statistics recording 6 drug-related deaths involving mephedrone, confirmed by toxicology, among 2,747 drug-related deaths in England and Wales in 2010, 2 of them with mephedrone as the only drug found, without giving the definition used (as cited by Forsyth, 2012). The 18 deaths are the media's selection, not a count of deaths involving mephedrone, and the outcome of each is as later reported, not taken from coroners' records; how many deaths blamed on mephedrone were confirmed in national registers is in the answer on confirmed mephedrone deaths. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Did news stories about mephedrone deaths get the facts right? Not always. In 2009 and 2010, online news in the UK linked 18 named deaths to mephedrone. Later reports said mephedrone was not found in 4 of them, was found but did not cause the death in 4, and played a part in 7, mostly together with other drugs or illnesses. The two deaths most linked to mephedrone online were later found to be from alcohol and methadone, and the first death in the news was reported as natural causes within a month. Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths were in the news. The author thinks the news raised interest in the drug, but search data cannot show that the news made people use it. This comes from one study, and the later test results are second-hand reports, not official records.
magnitude: Forsyth (2012), 18 named deaths linked to mephedrone in online news (26 November 2009 to about April 2011; suicides and violent or accidental deaths excluded, number not given). Later reports (second-hand): not detected 4; detected, not a factor 4; detected and a factor 7 (6 with other drugs or conditions alleged); no toxicology note 3 (one reported as natural causes); editors' tally of Table 1 notes. Most-linked cases: 9,060 and 8,730 web pages (Scunthorpe; alcohol and methadone at inquest). Cited from ONS: 6 toxicologically confirmed mephedrone-related deaths among 2,747 drug-related deaths, England and Wales, 2010; mephedrone the only drug in 2. Search data are relative indices without absolute numbers, with no 'mephedrone buy' data after 24 March 2010.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence checklist, high risk of bias (card sc_forsyth_2012): the 18 deaths are those online news named and Google News indexed, with suicides and violent deaths excluded uncounted; each death's outcome is as later reported, not taken from records; the search data are normalised screenshots; one author, no second coder.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the claim concerns online news about these deaths in one scare, as the study does.

grade.reasoning: A case series of deaths named in the news, starting low as observational evidence; down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision: very low. The claim rests only on this case series, whose toxicology is second-hand (as later reported, not from records), so it stays at draft and says its figures are illustrative (brief; METHODS §6.3). The search-interest findings are co-occurrence in screenshots and are reported as not showing cause, as the author concedes, although he reads them as suggesting that news of the deaths raised interest in the drug. Status single study; the project's reading list found no other study comparing news reports of individual drug deaths with later inquest or toxicology findings. The national register series of deaths blamed on mephedrone is a separate answer.
